title: Official Indonesian — notices, forms and the formal email
goal: Read the language of signs, forms and counters (*harap, dimohon, wajib, dilarang*), deal with a bank in standard Indonesian, and write a short formal email with the fixed openings and closings (*Yth., Dengan hormat, Hormat kami*).
bekal: understand and obey notices: *Harap antre*, *Dilarang merokok*, *Wajib lapor 1x24 jam*
open a bank account and fill in a form in formal Indonesian
write a formal email that starts with *Yth.* and *Dengan hormat* and ends with *Hormat kami*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Buka rekening di bank
dialogs.intro: A few days later. While her KITAS extension is being processed, Sarah needs an Indonesian bank account for her salary. She goes to a bank branch on Jalan Sudirman in Yogyakarta, where a security guard greets everyone at the door.

notes: **Harap — "kindly, you are expected to".** On signs and in official speech, *harap* + verb is a polite instruction that is not really optional: *Harap menunggu* (please wait), *Harap tenang* (quiet, please). It comes from *harap*, "to hope", but the hope is the institution's, and firm.

**Dilarang — "forbidden".** The standard prohibition on every sign in the country: *Dilarang merokok*, *Dilarang parkir*, *Dilarang masuk*. Sarah reads the sign aloud — a good habit, because notice Indonesian uses full *me-* verbs (*menggunakan*) and formal nouns (*telepon genggam* for *HP*) that you rarely hear in speech.

**Wajib — "compulsory, required".** *Wajib* is stronger than *harus* and implies a rule rather than a personal need: *Wajib melampirkan paspor*, *wajib diisi* (must be filled in). The mirror image on a form is *tidak wajib* or *opsional*.

**Ingin, membuka, melampirkan.** Sarah says *saya mau buka rekening* to the guard but *saya ingin membuka rekening tabungan* at the desk. *Ingin* is the formal "wish to", and the full *me-* verb goes with it. Both are correct; the second simply matches the room.

**Nama ibu kandung** — your biological mother's name — is asked on almost every Indonesian bank and government form as a security question. *Kandung* means "of the womb": *ibu kandung, saudara kandung* (full sibling). Foreigners are often surprised; Indonesians are surprised that anyone is surprised.

**BPJS Kesehatan** is the national health insurance scheme; foreigners who work in Indonesia for more than six months are required to join, usually through their employer. *HRD* (said *ha-ér-dé*) is the human resources department, the office that sorts it out.

grammars.title: Notice words: how strong is it?
body: Official Indonesian has a ladder of instructions, from a gentle request to a flat ban. These words start almost every sign, form and announcement.
after: Signs drop the subject and often the object: *Dilarang parkir* (no parking), *Harap lepas alas kaki* (please remove footwear). Who is forbidden? You are.
⚠️ Don't write *Tidak boleh parkir* on a sign — it is correct but sounds like a neighbour's note, not a notice.

grammars.title: Counter Indonesian and street Indonesian
body: At a bank, an office or an embassy, standard Indonesian is expected — from you and from the staff. Here are the swaps to make.
after: The pattern is always the same: full *me-* verbs, *tidak* not *nggak*, no particles (*sih, dong, kok*), and *Bapak/Ibu* for "you". That is most of what "formal Indonesian" means at A2.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Email resmi
dialogs.intro: Back at the office. Pak Hendra's visit is confirmed, and he wants to see one of the partner schools. Sarah has to write to its head teacher, Ibu Wulan Sari, and asks Mbak Nur to look at her draft.

notes: **Yth.** is short for *Yang terhormat*, "the honourable", and heads every formal letter or email before the recipient's title and name: *Yth. Bapak Hendra Wijaya*. It is always abbreviated in writing but read out in full at ceremonies.

**Dengan hormat,** ("with respect") is the fixed greeting of the formal letter, the equivalent of "Dear Sir or Madam". It stands alone on its own line, followed by a comma, and the letter starts on the next line.

**Kami bermaksud…** — "we intend to, we would like to". Formal letters speak for the institution with *kami*, not *saya*, even when one person is writing. *Bermaksud* (from *maksud*, intention) is the standard way to state the purpose of a letter.

**Mengunjungi sekolah Ibu.** In the email, *Ibu* means "you" and *sekolah Ibu* "your school". Formal Indonesian never uses *Anda* to someone it knows and respects; the title does the work. Capitalise it: *Ibu*, *Bapak*.

**Atas perhatian… kami ucapkan terima kasih.** The closing formula thanks the reader for their *perhatian* (attention) and often their *kerja sama* (cooperation). The word order — thanks at the end — is fixed; you will see it at the bottom of a thousand letters.

**Hormat kami — "yours faithfully".** Literally "our respect", it goes above your name and *jabatan* (job title). 💬 Among colleagues who email each other daily, *Salam* or *Terima kasih* is enough; Mbak Nur's rule is that the first email to anyone outside is always the formal one.

grammars.title: The shape of a formal email
body: An Indonesian formal letter or email is built from fixed parts in a fixed order. Learn the formulas and you only have to write the middle.

after: *Kesediaan* (willingness) is from *sedia* (ready): asking for someone's *kesediaan* is more polite than asking them to do something. You will meet the full letter, with *Sehubungan dengan* and *Demikian*, in the B2 book.
